::: {.sl-container .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
# Introduction to Effect Schema {#_top .astro-np5lzwrf}
:::
::::

::::::::: {.content-panel .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
:::::::: {.sl-container .astro-2wc2n45z style="--borderTop: initial;--pageTitleDisplay: block;"}
::::::: sl-markdown-content
Welcome to the documentation for `effect/Schema`{dir="auto"}, a module
for defining and using schemas to validate and transform data in
TypeScript.

The `effect/Schema`{dir="auto"} module allows you to define a
`Schema<Type, Encoded, Requirements>`{dir="auto"} that provides a
blueprint for describing the structure and data types of your data. Once
defined, you can leverage this schema to perform a range of operations,
including:

  Operation         Description
  ----------------- -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Decoding          Transforming data from an input type `Encoded`{dir="auto"} to an output type `Type`{dir="auto"}.
  Encoding          Converting data from an output type `Type`{dir="auto"} back to an input type `Encoded`{dir="auto"}.
  Asserting         Verifying that a value adheres to the schema's output type `Type`{dir="auto"}.
  Standard Schema   Generate a [Standard Schema V1](https://standardschema.dev/).
  Arbitraries       Generate arbitraries for [fast-check](https://github.com/dubzzz/fast-check) testing.
  JSON Schemas      Create JSON Schemas based on defined schemas.
  Equivalence       Create [Equivalence](../equivalence/index.html) based on defined schemas.
  Pretty printing   Support pretty printing for data structures.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## Requirements

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#requirements){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="requirements"}
:::

- TypeScript 5.4 or newer.
- The `strict`{dir="auto"} flag enabled in your
  `tsconfig.json`{dir="auto"} file.
- (Optional) The `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`{dir="auto"} flag enabled
  in your `tsconfig.json`{dir="auto"} file.

### The exactOptionalPropertyTypes Option

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#the-exactoptionalpropertytypes-option){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="the-exactoptionalpropertytypes-option"}
:::

The `effect/Schema`{dir="auto"} module takes advantage of the
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`{dir="auto"} option of
`tsconfig.json`{dir="auto"}. This option affects how optional properties
are typed (to learn more about this option, you can refer to the
official [TypeScript
documentation](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig#exactOptionalPropertyTypes)).

Here, notice that the type of `name`{dir="auto"} is "exact"
(`string`{dir="auto"}), which means the type checker will catch any
attempt to assign an invalid value (like `undefined`{dir="auto"}).

**Example** (With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`{dir="auto"} Disabled)

If, for some reason, you can't enable the
`exactOptionalPropertyTypes`{dir="auto"} option (perhaps due to
conflicts with other third-party libraries), you can still use
`effect/Schema`{dir="auto"}. However, there will be a mismatch between
the types and the runtime behavior:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame not-content">
<pre data-language="ts"><code>1import { Schema } from &quot;effect&quot;2
3const Person = Schema.Struct({4  name: Schema.optionalWith(Schema.NonEmptyString, { exact: true })5})6
7type Type = Schema.Schema.Type&lt;typeof Person&gt;8/*9type Type = {10    readonly name?: string | undefined;11}12*/13
14// No type error, but a decoding failure occurs15Schema.decodeSync(Person)({ name: undefined })16/*17throws:18ParseError: { readonly name?: NonEmptyString }19└─ [&quot;name&quot;]20   └─ NonEmptyString21      └─ From side refinement failure22         └─ Expected string, actual undefined23*/</code></pre>
<div class="copy">
<div>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
:::

In this case, the type of `name`{dir="auto"} is widened to
`string | undefined`{dir="auto"}, which means the type checker won't
catch the invalid value (`undefined`{dir="auto"}). However, during
decoding, you'll encounter an error, indicating that
`undefined`{dir="auto"} is not allowed.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## The Schema Type

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#the-schema-type){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="the-schema-type"}
:::

A schema is an immutable value that describes the structure of your
data, and it is represented by the `Schema`{dir="auto"} type.

Here is the general form of a `Schema`{dir="auto"}:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame not-content">
<pre data-language="text"><code>         ┌─── Type of the decoded value         │        ┌─── Encoded type (input/output)         │        │      ┌─── Requirements (context)         ▼        ▼      ▼Schema&lt;Type, Encoded, Requirements&gt;</code></pre>
<div class="copy">
<div>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
:::

The `Schema`{dir="auto"} type has three type parameters with the
following meanings:

  Parameter          Description
  ------------------ ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Type**           Represents the type of value that a schema can succeed with during decoding.
  **Encoded**        Represents the type of value that a schema can succeed with during encoding. By default, it's equal to `Type`{dir="auto"} if not explicitly provided.
  **Requirements**   Similar to the [`Effect`{dir="auto"}](../../getting-started/the-effect-type.html) type, it represents the contextual data required by the schema to execute both decoding and encoding. If this type parameter is `never`{dir="auto"} (default if not explicitly provided), it means the schema has no requirements.

**Examples**

- `Schema<string>`{dir="auto"} (defaulted to
  `Schema<string, string, never>`{dir="auto"}) represents a schema that
  decodes to `string`{dir="auto"}, encodes to `string`{dir="auto"}, and
  has no requirements.
- `Schema<number, string>`{dir="auto"} (defaulted to
  `Schema<number, string, never>`{dir="auto"}) represents a schema that
  decodes to `number`{dir="auto"} from `string`{dir="auto"}, encodes a
  `number`{dir="auto"} to a `string`{dir="auto"}, and has no
  requirements.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){.starlight-aside__icon
.astro-4rgy7crp} Type Parameter Abbreviations

::: starlight-aside__content
In the Effect ecosystem, you may often encounter the type parameters of
`Schema`{dir="auto"} abbreviated as `A`{dir="auto"}, `I`{dir="auto"},
and `R`{dir="auto"} respectively. This is just shorthand for the type
value of type **A**, **I**nput, and **R**equirements.
:::

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## Understanding Schema Values

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#understanding-schema-values){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="understanding-schema-values"}
:::

**Immutability**. `Schema`{dir="auto"} values are immutable, and every
function in the `effect/Schema`{dir="auto"} module produces a new
`Schema`{dir="auto"} value.

**Modeling Data Structure**. These values do not perform any actions
themselves, they simply model or describe the structure of your data.

**Interpretation by Compilers**. A `Schema`{dir="auto"} can be
interpreted by various "compilers" into specific operations, depending
on the compiler type (decoding, encoding, pretty printing, arbitraries,
etc...).

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## Understanding Decoding and Encoding

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#understanding-decoding-and-encoding){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="understanding-decoding-and-encoding"}
:::

When working with data in TypeScript, you often need to handle data
coming from or being sent to external systems. This data may not always
match the format or types you expect, especially when dealing with user
input, data from APIs, or data stored in different formats. To handle
these discrepancies, we use **decoding** and **encoding**.

  Term           Description
  -------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Decoding**   Used for parsing data from external sources where you have no control over the data format.
  **Encoding**   Used when sending data out to external sources, converting it to a format that is expected by those sources.

For instance, when working with forms in the frontend, you often receive
untyped data in the form of strings. This data can be tampered with and
does not natively support arrays or booleans. Decoding helps you
validate and parse this data into more useful types like numbers, dates,
and arrays. Encoding allows you to convert these types back into the
string format expected by forms.

Below is a diagram that shows the relationship between encoding and
decoding using a `Schema<A, I, R>`{dir="auto"}:

::: expressive-code
<figure class="frame not-content">
<pre data-language="text"><code>┌─────────┐       ┌───┐       ┌───┐       ┌─────────┐| unknown |       | A |       | I |       | unknown |└─────────┘       └───┘       └───┘       └─────────┘     |              |           |              |     | validate     |           |              |     |─────────────►│           |              |     |              |           |              |     | is           |           |              |     |─────────────►│           |              |     |              |           |              |     | asserts      |           |              |     |─────────────►│           |              |     |              |           |              |     | encodeUnknown|           |              |     |─────────────────────────►|              |                    |           |              |                    | encode    |              |                    |──────────►│              |                    |           |              |                    |    decode |              |                    | ◄─────────|              |                    |           |              |                    |           | decodeUnknown|                    | ◄────────────────────────|</code></pre>
<div class="copy">
<div>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
:::

We'll break down these concepts using an example with a
`Schema<Date, string, never>`{dir="auto"}. This schema serves as a tool
to transform a `string`{dir="auto"} into a `Date`{dir="auto"} and vice
versa.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h3 tabindex="-1"}
### Encoding

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#encoding){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="encoding"}
:::

When we talk about "encoding," we are referring to the process of
changing a `Date`{dir="auto"} into a `string`{dir="auto"}. To put it
simply, it's the act of converting data from one format to another.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h3 tabindex="-1"}
### Decoding

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#decoding){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="decoding"}
:::

Conversely, "decoding" entails transforming a `string`{dir="auto"} back
into a `Date`{dir="auto"}. It's essentially the reverse operation of
encoding, where data is returned to its original form.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h3 tabindex="-1"}
### Decoding From Unknown

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#decoding-from-unknown){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="decoding-from-unknown"}
:::

Decoding from `unknown`{dir="auto"} involves two key steps:

1.  **Checking:** Initially, we verify that the input data (which is of
    the `unknown`{dir="auto"} type) matches the expected structure. In
    our specific case, this means ensuring that the input is indeed a
    `string`{dir="auto"}.

2.  **Decoding:** Following the successful check, we proceed to convert
    the `string`{dir="auto"} into a `Date`{dir="auto"}. This process
    completes the decoding operation, where the data is both validated
    and transformed.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h3 tabindex="-1"}
### Encoding From Unknown

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#encoding-from-unknown){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="encoding-from-unknown"}
:::

Encoding from `unknown`{dir="auto"} involves two key steps:

1.  **Checking:** Initially, we verify that the input data (which is of
    the `unknown`{dir="auto"} type) matches the expected structure. In
    our specific case, this means ensuring that the input is indeed a
    `Date`{dir="auto"}.

2.  **Encoding:** Following the successful check, we proceed to convert
    the `Date`{dir="auto"} into a `string`{dir="auto"}. This process
    completes the encoding operation, where the data is both validated
    and transformed.

::: {.autolink-heading-container .level-h2 tabindex="-1"}
## The Rule of Schemas

[[![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)]{.anchor-icon
aria-hidden="true"}](index.html#the-rule-of-schemas){.anchor-link
aria-labelledby="the-rule-of-schemas"}
:::

When working with schemas, there's an important rule to keep in mind:
your schemas should be crafted in a way that when you perform both
encoding and decoding operations, you should end up with the original
value.

In simpler terms, if you encode a value and then immediately decode it,
the result should match the original value you started with. This rule
ensures that your data remains consistent and reliable throughout the
encoding and decoding process.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){.starlight-aside__icon
.astro-4rgy7crp} Ensure Consistency

::: starlight-aside__content
As a general rule, schemas should be defined such that encode + decode
return the original value.
:::
